tool.name: pathlib
tool.tagline: Object-oriented file system paths that work the same on every OS
tool.description: pathlib represents file system paths as objects with methods for joining, inspecting, reading, writing, globbing and resolving them. It replaces most uses of os.path, glob and open with one readable API that handles Windows and POSIX differences. It's the modern default for any Python code that touches files.

glossary.def: pathlib's type for a file path: an object that can join, take apart and inspect paths, and read and write the files they point to.
A pathlib path that only works on the path's text (joining, splitting, matching) and never touches the disk, so it can handle another operating system's paths.
A pathlib path (Path, PosixPath, WindowsPath) that can also read, write and inspect real files on this computer.
Any object that can give its file path as a string through an __fspath__ method, such as a Path. Most of Python's file functions accept one.
In a walk through folders: cutting whole branches out, so the folders below them are never visited at all.
An attack where a file name supplied by a user, like ../../secret.txt, escapes the folder the program meant to allow.
Asking the operating system for a file's details (size, last change time, permissions); in Python, p.stat() or os.stat().

concepts.name: Path objects and the / operator
concepts.summary: Create Path objects, join them with /, and find the current folder and your home folder.
concepts.why: Path objects make file code shorter, easier to read and the same on every computer, compared with gluing strings together.
concepts.body:
A file path is text like `data/input.csv`. Windows writes it with backslashes (`data\input.csv`), Mac and Linux with forward slashes. pathlib gives you a **Path** type that handles those differences for you. Write `from pathlib import Path`, then `Path("data/input.csv")` creates a path object. Behind the scenes it becomes a `WindowsPath` on Windows and a `PosixPath` elsewhere, but you rarely need to care.

Join paths with the **/ operator**:

```python
base = Path("data")
report = base / "2024" / "report.csv"
```

Strings can be on either side (`"logs" / Path("x")` works too), and the right separator is used for your system. One surprise: joining an **absolute path** (one that starts from the very top of the disk, like `/etc` or `C:\`) throws away what came before: `Path("data") / "/etc"` is `/etc`.

Useful starting points:

- `Path.cwd()` the **working directory**: the folder your program is currently "in", where plain file names are looked up
- `Path.home()` your **home directory**: your personal folder, like `/home/ann` or `C:\Users\ann`
- `Path(__file__).parent` the folder containing the current `.py` file: the reliable base for files that come with your code

`str(p)` turns a path back into a string when some code really needs one. But nearly all of the standard library (`open`, `os`, `shutil`, `json`...) accepts Path objects directly.

Paths are **immutable**: methods return new paths. Like strings, they can be dict keys or set members. Comparing paths compares their parts; on Windows, capital and small letters count as the same.
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path

base = Path("data")
report = base / "2024" / "report.csv"
print(report)                    # data/2024/report.csv
print(type(report).__name__)     # PosixPath
print(Path("data") / "/etc")     # /etc

print(Path.home().is_absolute())  # True
print(Path.cwd() == Path(".").resolve())  # True

seen = {Path("a/b"), Path("a") / "b"}
print(len(seen))                 # 1
here = Path(__file__).parent if "__file__" in globals() else Path.cwd()
print(here.is_dir())             # True
takeaways: `Path(...) / 'name'` joins paths the right way on every system
`Path.cwd()`, `Path.home()` and `Path(__file__).parent` are common starting points
Paths are immutable and accepted by open, os and shutil
pitfalls: Concatenating strings with '/' and passing them around instead of keeping Path objects.

quiz.explain: The / operator joins the pieces with the system's separator and returns a new Path that doesn't start at the top of the disk.

concepts.name: Names, suffixes and parents
concepts.summary: Take paths apart with name, stem, suffix, parent and parts, and derive new paths with with_name, with_stem and with_suffix.
concepts.why: Renaming outputs, grouping files by extension and finding sibling files are everyday tasks.
concepts.body:
A path gives you its pieces as attributes (values you read with a dot, no brackets). They are all worked out from the path's text, without looking at the disk:

- `p.name` the last part: `report.tar.gz`
- `p.suffix` the last **file extension** (the ending after a dot, which hints at the file type): `.gz`; `p.suffixes`: `['.tar', '.gz']`
- `p.stem` the name without the last suffix: `report.tar`
- `p.parent` the folder it's in; `p.parents` all the folders above it, nearest first (`p.parents[1]` is the one above the parent)
- `p.parts` a tuple of all the pieces; `p.anchor` the starting point (`/`, or a drive like `C:\`)

To make related paths, use the `with_*` methods, which return new paths:

- `p.with_suffix(".json")` replaces the last suffix (pass `""` to remove it)
- `p.with_name("other.txt")` replaces the last part
- `p.with_stem("report-v2")` keeps the suffix and changes the stem

Typical pattern: `out = src.with_suffix(".processed.csv")`, or put output next to the input with `src.parent / f"{src.stem}.out"`.

Gotchas: `suffix` only sees the last dot, so `.tar.gz` needs `suffixes`. A name that starts with a dot, like `.bashrc`, has no suffix (its stem is `.bashrc`). The parent of a single name is `Path(".")` (the current folder), and the parent of `/` is `/` itself.
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("/srv/backups/db.2025-03-01.tar.gz")
print(p.name)            # db.2025-03-01.tar.gz
print(p.stem)            # db.2025-03-01.tar
print(p.suffix)          # .gz
print(p.suffixes)        # ['.2025-03-01', '.tar', '.gz']
print(p.parent)          # /srv/backups
print(p.parents[1])      # /srv
print(p.parts[:3])       # ('/', 'srv', 'backups')

src = Path("photos/cat.jpeg")
print(src.with_suffix(".png"))     # photos/cat.png
print(src.with_stem("cat_small"))  # photos/cat_small.jpeg
print(Path(".bashrc").suffix == "")  # True
print(Path("notes.txt").parent)    # .
takeaways: `name`, `stem`, `suffix`, `parent` and `parts` only read the path's text; they don't touch the disk
`with_suffix`, `with_name` and `with_stem` make new paths
Dots in names are tricky: use `suffixes` for extensions with several parts
pitfalls: Expecting `suffix` to return '.tar.gz'; it only returns the last extension.

quiz.explain: with_suffix replaces only the last suffix, '.gz'.

concepts.name: Reading and writing files
concepts.summary: Read and write whole files with read_text, write_text, read_bytes and write_bytes, or open a Path to go through a file line by line.
concepts.why: Small files can be read or written in one call, without the usual open-and-close code.
concepts.body:
For small and medium files, Path has one-call helpers:

- `p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")` returns the whole file as a str.
- `p.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")` creates or **overwrites** the file and returns the number of characters written.
- `p.read_bytes()` and `p.write_bytes(data)` do the same with bytes, for images and other files that aren't text.

Each call opens and closes the file for you. Always pass `encoding=` for text: the default is your computer's own setting, which differs between machines (Python 3.15 will switch to UTF-8 by default). `read_text` in 3.13 also accepts `newline=`.

For large files, or to go through a file one line at a time, use `p.open()`, which takes the same arguments as the built-in `open`:

```python
with p.open(encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        ...
```

`write_text` doesn't create missing folders. Call `p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` first; it creates the folder and any missing folders above it. To add to the end of a file, use `p.open("a")`; there is no `append_text`.

`read_text` loads the whole file into memory at once. That's ideal for settings files and other small text files, but avoid it for huge files.
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path

out = Path("build") / "hello.txt"
out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
print(out.write_text("héllo\nworld\n", encoding="utf-8"))  # 12
print(out.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines())  # ['héllo', 'world']
print(len(out.read_bytes()))      # 13  (é is 2 bytes in UTF-8)

with out.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:   # add to the end
    f.write("again\n")

with out.open(encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.rstrip("\n"))  # héllo, then world, then again
takeaways: `read_text`/`write_text` open and close the file in one call
Always pass `encoding="utf-8"` for text files
Use `p.open()` for large files, reading line by line, or adding to the end
pitfalls: Calling `write_text` on a path whose folder doesn't exist yet; it raises FileNotFoundError.

quiz.q: What does Path('log.txt').write_text('new') do if log.txt already has content?
quiz.explain: write_text opens the file in 'w' mode, which empties it first.

concepts.name: Checking and listing paths
concepts.summary: Check whether paths exist and what they are, and list a folder's contents with iterdir.
concepts.why: Scripts constantly need to know whether an input exists and what files a folder holds.
concepts.body:
These methods look at the actual disk, through the **file system** (the way your computer organises files and folders). A folder is also called a **directory**, hence the `dir` in the names:

- `p.exists()` true if anything is there
- `p.is_file()`, `p.is_dir()`, `p.is_symlink()`
- `p.stat().st_size` size in bytes, `p.stat().st_mtime` when it was last changed (as a number of seconds)

A **symlink** (symbolic link) is a small file that just points to another file or folder, like a desktop shortcut. These methods return `False` rather than raising an error when the path is missing or you aren't allowed to see it. Since 3.12, `exists`, `is_file` and `is_dir` take `follow_symlinks=False` to look at a link itself rather than what it points to.

`p.iterdir()` gives a Path for each entry in the folder, already joined with `p`, in no particular order. You get usable paths, not bare names:

```python
csvs = []
for f in folder.iterdir():
    if f.suffix == ".csv":
        csvs.append(f)
```

`iterdir` raises `NotADirectoryError` if `p` is a file and `FileNotFoundError` if it's missing.

Checking first is fine for friendly messages ("input file not found"), but it isn't airtight: another program can delete the file between `exists()` and `read_text()`. When it matters, just try the operation and catch `FileNotFoundError`.

To list the contents of folders inside folders too, use `glob`/`rglob` or `Path.walk()` (later lessons) instead of nesting `iterdir` calls by hand.
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("inbox")
folder.mkdir()
for name in ["b.csv", "a.csv", "readme.md"]:
    (folder / name).write_text("x", encoding="utf-8")
(folder / "archive").mkdir()

print(folder.exists(), folder.is_dir())          # True True
names = []
for p in folder.iterdir():
    names.append(p.name)
print(sorted(names))         # ['a.csv', 'archive', 'b.csv', 'readme.md']

csvs = []
for p in folder.iterdir():
    if p.is_file() and p.suffix == ".csv":
        csvs.append(p)
print(sorted(csvs))  # [PosixPath('inbox/a.csv'), PosixPath('inbox/b.csv')]
print((folder / "nope.txt").exists())            # False
print((folder / "a.csv").stat().st_size)         # 1
takeaways: `exists`, `is_file` and `is_dir` return False instead of raising
`iterdir()` gives full Path objects in no particular order
When correctness matters, try the operation and catch the error instead of checking first
pitfalls: Assuming iterdir lists files in alphabetical order; it doesn't, so sort them.

quiz.q: folder = Path('docs'). What does next(folder.iterdir()) return if docs contains intro.md?
quiz.explain: iterdir gives paths already joined with the folder, ready to open.

concepts.name: Globbing with glob and rglob
concepts.summary: Find files by pattern with glob, and search every folder below with rglob or **.
concepts.why: Collecting inputs like 'every .py file in the project' is a one-liner with glob.
concepts.body:
`p.glob(pattern)` gives the paths below `p` that match a **glob pattern**: a file-name pattern with wildcards, the same kind you can type in a terminal.

- `*` matches any characters within one part of the path
- `?` matches one character; `[abc]` one of a set of characters
- `**` matches any number of folders, including none

So `p.glob("*.csv")` searches one folder, `p.glob("**/*.csv")` that folder and every folder below it, and `p.rglob("*.csv")` is short for the latter (the r stands for "recursive"). Results come in no particular order; sort them for stable output.

Details worth knowing:

- Hidden files (names starting with `.`) are matched by `*`, unlike in most terminals.
- Whether capital letters matter follows your system's rules by default; pass `case_sensitive=True/False` (3.12+) to choose.
- In 3.13, a pattern ending in `**` gives both files and folders; earlier versions gave only folders. Add `/*` or a suffix like `*.py` if you want files only.
- `glob` hands out its results one at a time, and only once; wrap it in `list()` or `sorted()` to keep them.
- `**` doesn't follow symlinks to folders unless you pass `recurse_symlinks=True` (3.13).

To skip folders such as `.git` or `node_modules`, filter the results (`".git" not in p.parts`), or use `Path.walk()`, where you can skip whole branches for speed.
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path

for f in ["src/app.py", "src/util/io.py", "src/util/README.md",
          "tests/test_app.py", ".venv/lib/x.py"]:
    p = Path(f)
    p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    p.touch()

root = Path(".")
print(sorted(map(str, root.glob("src/*.py"))))   # ['src/app.py']
py = sorted(str(p) for p in root.rglob("*.py") if ".venv" not in p.parts)
print(py)    # ['src/app.py', 'src/util/io.py', 'tests/test_app.py']
print(sorted(p.name for p in root.glob("**/test_*.py")))  # ['test_app.py']
print(len(list(root.glob("src/util/*.MD", case_sensitive=False))))  # 1
takeaways: `glob('*.ext')` searches one folder; `rglob('*.ext')` or `glob('**/*.ext')` every folder below
Results come unordered and only once; sort and list them as needed
Filter by `p.parts` or use `Path.walk` to skip folders like .git
pitfalls: Expecting `glob('*.py')` to search folders inside the folder; it only looks one level deep.

quiz.q: Which call finds config.yaml files in a folder and all the folders below it?
quiz.explain: rglob puts **/ in front of the pattern, so it searches every folder below.

concepts.name: Creating, moving and deleting
concepts.summary: Make folders, create empty files, rename, replace and delete files and empty folders with Path methods.
concepts.why: Output folders, temp files and archiving steps are part of nearly every script.
concepts.body:
Path wraps the common file operations:

- `p.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` creates the folder and any missing folders above it, and doesn't complain if it already exists.
- `p.touch()` creates an empty file or updates its last-changed time; `touch(exist_ok=False)` fails if it exists.
- `p.rename(target)` moves or renames and returns the new Path. On Windows it fails if `target` exists.
- `p.replace(target)` does the same but overwrites `target` on every system. On Mac and Linux the swap happens in one step, so other programs never see a half-done state.
- `p.unlink(missing_ok=True)` deletes a file, doing nothing if it's already gone.
- `p.rmdir()` deletes an **empty** folder.

A relative target in `rename` and `replace` is taken relative to the working directory, not to `p`'s folder. Write `p.rename(p.with_name("new.txt"))` or `p.parent / "new.txt"` to stay in the same folder.

In 3.13 pathlib can't delete or copy a whole folder with everything inside. Use `shutil.rmtree(p)`, `shutil.copy2(src, dst)` and `shutil.move(src, dst)`, which all accept Path objects. (Python 3.14 adds `Path.copy` and `Path.move`.)

All these methods raise the usual file errors, which are all kinds of `OSError`: `FileExistsError`, `FileNotFoundError`, `IsADirectoryError`, `PermissionError`.
concepts.code:
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

out = Path("out/2025/03")
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
draft = out / "draft.txt"
draft.write_text("v1", encoding="utf-8")

final = draft.rename(draft.with_name("final.txt"))   # same folder
print(final)                          # out/2025/03/final.txt
print(draft.exists())                 # False

(out / "tmp.lock").touch()
(out / "tmp.lock").unlink()
(out / "tmp.lock").unlink(missing_ok=True)   # no error when absent

try:
    Path("out").rmdir()
except OSError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)           # OSError
shutil.rmtree("out")
print(Path("out").exists())           # False
takeaways: `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` makes sure a folder exists
`rename` targets are relative to the working directory; build them from `p.parent` or `with_name`
Use shutil to delete or copy whole folders and to move files between disks
pitfalls: Writing `p.rename('new.txt')` and finding the file moved into the working directory.

quiz.q: p = Path('data/raw/a.csv'). Where does p.rename('b.csv') put the file?
options: b.csv in the current working directory
quiz.explain: A relative target is taken relative to the working directory, not the file's own folder.

concepts.name: Absolute, resolved and relative paths
concepts.summary: Turn paths into full, clean paths with resolve and absolute, expand ~, and get the part of a path below a base folder with relative_to.
concepts.why: Comparing paths, printing short names and checking that a path is inside a folder all need clean, full paths.
concepts.body:
Three ways to make a path absolute:

- `p.absolute()` puts the working directory in front. It leaves `..` (meaning "the folder above") and symlinks (files that point to another file or folder) alone.
- `p.resolve()` makes it absolute **and** removes `..` and follows symlinks, giving the one true location. Use it before comparing paths or checking that one is inside another. With `strict=True` it raises an error if the path doesn't exist.
- `p.expanduser()` replaces a leading `~` with your home directory. Paths never expand `~` by themselves.

`p.relative_to(base)` returns the part of `p` below `base`: `Path("/srv/app/static/a.css").relative_to("/srv/app")` gives `static/a.css`. It raises `ValueError` if `p` isn't under `base`. Since 3.12, `walk_up=True` allows answers that start with `..`.

`p.is_relative_to(base)` returns True or False instead of raising, but it only compares the **text** of the parts, not real locations: `Path("/srv/app/../etc")` "is relative to" `/srv/app`. Resolve both sides first when the path comes from users.

`p.samefile(other)` checks whether two paths point to the same file on disk, taking links into account.

Text-only cleanup like `os.path.normpath` has no direct pathlib version, because collapsing `a/link/..` without looking at the disk can be wrong when `link` is a symlink.
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path

Path("site/static").mkdir(parents=True)
Path("site/static/a.css").touch()
Path("site/latest").symlink_to("static")

p = Path("site/static/../static/a.css")
print(p.absolute() == Path.cwd() / p)          # True: no normalisation
print(p.resolve() == Path.cwd() / "site/static/a.css")   # True
print(Path("site/latest/a.css").resolve().parent.name)   # static

print(Path("/srv/app/static/a.css").relative_to("/srv/app"))  # static/a.css
print(Path("/srv/app").relative_to("/srv/app/static", walk_up=True))  # ..
print(Path("/srv/app/../etc").is_relative_to("/srv/app"))   # True (!)
print(Path("~/notes").expanduser().is_absolute())           # True
takeaways: `resolve()` gives the true location: absolute, no `..`, symlinks followed
`relative_to` strips a base folder and raises if the path isn't under it
`is_relative_to` compares text only; resolve paths from users first
pitfalls: Treating `Path('~/x')` as the home folder without calling `expanduser()`.

quiz.q: Which call gives a clean, full path suitable for checking whether two paths refer to the same location?
quiz.explain: resolve makes the path absolute and removes .. parts and symlinks.

concepts.name: Walking trees and file metadata
concepts.summary: Go through whole folder trees with Path.walk, skip unwanted branches, and use stat results for size- and age-based jobs.
concepts.why: Cleanup jobs, disk-usage reports and build scripts need to visit every file along with its metadata (size, dates).
concepts.body:
`Path.walk()` (3.12+) is pathlib's version of `os.walk`. It gives `(dirpath, dirnames, filenames)` for each folder, with `dirpath` as a Path and the other two as lists of names:

```python
for root, dirs, files in Path("proj").walk():
    dirs[:] = [d for d in dirs if d not in {".git", "node_modules"}]
```

Changing `dirs` in place **prunes** the walk: it cuts off those branches. That is much faster than filtering `rglob` results afterwards, because pruned folders are never listed at all. Use `top_down=False` to visit the folders inside before the folder itself (needed when deleting folders), and `on_error=` to handle folders you can't read; by default such errors are ignored.

Each file's details come from `path.stat()`, a **stat** call that asks the operating system for them:

- `st_size` in bytes
- `st_mtime` when it was last changed, as a Unix timestamp (seconds since 1970); compare with `time.time()` or convert with `datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, tz=timezone.utc)`

A typical maintenance job, "delete log files older than 30 days", combines `walk` or `glob`, `stat().st_mtime` and `unlink`.

`p.stat()` follows symlinks; `p.lstat()` (or `stat(follow_symlinks=False)`) describes the link itself. `p.owner()` and `p.group()` give names on Mac and Linux, and `p.chmod(0o644)` changes the file permissions.
concepts.code:
import os
import time
from pathlib import Path

for f in ["logs/app.log", "logs/old/2023.log", ".git/HEAD"]:
    Path(f).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    Path(f).write_text("x" * 100, encoding="utf-8")
month_ago = time.time() - 31 * 86400
os.utime("logs/old/2023.log", (month_ago, month_ago))

sizes, stale = {}, []
for root, dirs, files in Path(".").walk():
    dirs[:] = [d for d in dirs if not d.startswith(".")]     # prune .git
    for name in files:
        st = (root / name).stat()
        sizes[str(root / name)] = st.st_size
        if st.st_mtime < time.time() - 30 * 86400:
            stale.append(root / name)
print(sorted(sizes))      # ['logs/app.log', 'logs/old/2023.log']
print(stale)              # [PosixPath('logs/old/2023.log')]
takeaways: `Path.walk()` (3.12+) gives `(dirpath, dirnames, filenames)` like os.walk
Prune by changing `dirnames` in place; it skips whole branches
`stat().st_size` and `st_mtime` drive size- and age-based jobs
pitfalls: Using `rglob('*')` and filtering out `.git` afterwards on huge trees; the skipped folders are still fully searched.

quiz.q: Why is pruning dirnames in Path.walk faster than filtering rglob('*') results?
options: Pruned folders are never listed at all
quiz.explain: Removing a name from dirnames stops walk from going into that folder.

concepts.name: Pure paths and Windows vs POSIX
concepts.summary: Manipulate paths for another operating system with PurePosixPath and PureWindowsPath, without touching the disk.
concepts.why: Tools that build paths for other machines (cloud storage keys, paths on a remote Linux server, Windows shares from Linux) need the other system's rules.
concepts.body:
pathlib has two families of classes:

- **Pure paths** (`PurePath`, `PurePosixPath`, `PureWindowsPath`) only work on the path's text: joining, parts, suffixes, matching. They never touch the disk, so they work for any system's paths on any system.
- **Concrete paths** (`Path`, `PosixPath`, `WindowsPath`) add methods that read and change real files. You can only create the concrete class of your own operating system; `WindowsPath` on Linux raises `UnsupportedOperation` (3.13).

Use pure paths when the path isn't on this computer:

- `PurePosixPath("bucket") / "2025" / "a.csv"` for file names in cloud object storage (like Amazon S3) or paths on a remote Linux server, even when your code runs on Windows.
- `PureWindowsPath(r"C:\Users\ann\file.txt")` to take apart Windows paths that arrive in data on a Linux server.

Windows rules differ: both `\` and `/` are separators, drives and network shares form the `anchor` (`C:\`, `\\server\share\`), comparison ignores capital letters, and `p.as_posix()` converts to forward slashes.

`p.as_uri()` turns an absolute path into a `file://` URL (a web-style address for a local file), and since 3.13 `Path.from_uri()` turns one back.

Note that pure paths accept any string; they won't tell you a name is invalid on Windows (such as `CON` or one containing `:`).
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path, PurePosixPath, PureWindowsPath

w = PureWindowsPath(r"C:\Users\Ann\Docs/report.DOCX")
print(w.parts)        # ('C:\\', 'Users', 'Ann', 'Docs', 'report.DOCX')
print(w.drive, w.suffix)               # C: .DOCX
print(w.as_posix())                    # C:/Users/Ann/Docs/report.DOCX
print(w == PureWindowsPath(r"c:\users\ann\docs\REPORT.docx"))  # True

key = PurePosixPath("exports") / "2025" / "sales.csv"   # e.g. an S3 key
print(str(key))                        # exports/2025/sales.csv

uri = Path("/tmp/a b.txt").as_uri()
print(uri)                             # file:///tmp/a%20b.txt
print(Path.from_uri(uri))              # /tmp/a b.txt
takeaways: Pure paths do text-only path work for any system; concrete paths also read and write files
Use PurePosixPath for remote or cloud storage paths whatever your own system is
Windows paths ignore capital letters when compared and accept both slash styles
pitfalls: Using `Path` (and so local separators) to build S3 keys or remote Linux paths when code may run on Windows.

quiz.q: On Linux, what happens with PureWindowsPath('D:/data') / 'x.txt'?
options: It raises an error because Windows paths are unsupported
quiz.explain: Pure paths are platform-independent string manipulations, usable on any OS.

concepts.name: Matching paths and safe joins
concepts.summary: Test paths against glob patterns with match and full_match, and confine user-supplied paths to a base directory.
concepts.why: Sorting files into groups by pattern and stopping path traversal attacks are both matching problems.
concepts.body:
Two ways to test a path against a glob pattern without listing folders:

- `p.match(pattern)` matches **from the right** for relative patterns: `Path("a/b/c.py").match("*.py")` and `match("b/*.py")` are both true. `**` doesn't reach across folders here; it acts like `*`.
- `p.full_match(pattern)` (3.13) matches the **whole** path, and `**` spans any number of folders: `full_match("src/**/*.py")`. This is the one to use for rules like "ignore these files".

Both accept `case_sensitive=`.

Matching is also where **path traversal** bugs live: a name supplied by a user escapes the folder you meant to allow. If a web app serves `base / user_input`, then input like `../../etc/passwd`, or an absolute path, escapes the base. The safe recipe:

1. Join, then `resolve()` to remove `..` and follow symlinks.
2. Check `resolved.is_relative_to(base.resolve())`.
3. Reject otherwise.

Checking the string for `..` is not enough (absolute paths, symlinks, encoded separators). Also reject or clean up empty strings and the zero byte (`\x00`), which raise `ValueError` in file functions.

For archives (zip or tar files), the same check applies to every file name inside before unpacking; Python 3.12+ `tarfile` offers `filter="data"` (the default from 3.14) for exactly this.
concepts.code:
from pathlib import Path, PurePosixPath

p = PurePosixPath("src/pkg/util/io.py")
print(p.match("*.py"), p.match("util/*.py"))     # True True
print(p.match("src/*.py"))                       # False
print(p.full_match("src/**/*.py"))               # True
print(p.full_match("*.py"))                      # False

def safe_join(base, user_path):
    base = base.resolve()
    target = (base / user_path).resolve()
    if not target.is_relative_to(base):
        raise PermissionError(f"outside base: {user_path}")
    return target

Path("public/img").mkdir(parents=True)
print(safe_join(Path("public"), "img/logo.png").name)   # logo.png
for bad in ["../secret.txt", "/etc/passwd", "img/../../x"]:
    try:
        safe_join(Path("public"), bad)
    except PermissionError as e:
        print(e)
takeaways: `match` matches from the right; `full_match` (3.13) matches the whole path, with `**` across folders
Resolve, then check `is_relative_to(base)` to keep user paths inside a folder
String checks for '..' don't stop path traversal
pitfalls: Serving `base / requested_path` without resolving it and checking it's inside the base.

quiz.q: Which input does a check like `'..' not in user_path` fail to block?
quiz.explain: An absolute path contains no '..' but replaces the base entirely when joined.

concepts.name: Accepting paths in your own APIs
concepts.summary: Design functions that accept str, bytes and PathLike arguments correctly, with accurate type hints.
concepts.why: Library code that only works with one kind of path frustrates users and breaks in surprising ways.
concepts.body:
Callers will pass strings, Path objects, and occasionally other **os.PathLike** objects: anything with an `__fspath__` method that returns its path as a string (from libraries like `py.path`, or your own classes). A robust function accepts all of them:

```python
def load(path: str | os.PathLike[str]) -> dict:
    path = Path(path)
```

Rules of thumb:

- **Convert once, at the start**: turn the argument into `Path(path)` at the top of the function, then work with Path inside.
- If you need a string (for a C library or a subprocess argument), use `os.fspath(path)` rather than `str(path)`. `fspath` accepts only str, bytes and PathLike and raises `TypeError` for anything else, whereas `str()` happily turns `None` or an int into a bogus path.
- Type hints: `str | os.PathLike[str]` is the common annotation; typeshed (the collection of type hints for the standard library) has a `StrPath` alias meaning the same.
- **Return Path objects** from functions that produce paths; they convert to strings easily.
- Don't accept bytes paths unless you really need to handle file names that aren't valid text; mixing str and bytes in one join raises `TypeError`.

Avoid `isinstance(x, str)` checks to decide whether something is a path: a `str` might be the file's contents. Make two clearly named parameters or functions instead (`load_file(path)` vs `loads(text)`), the way `json` does.
concepts.code:
import os
from pathlib import Path

def word_count(path: str | os.PathLike[str]) -> int:
    path = Path(path)                       # normalise once
    return len(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").split())

class Asset:
    def __init__(self, name): self.name = name
    def __fspath__(self): return f"assets/{self.name}"

Path("assets").mkdir()
Path("assets/a.txt").write_text("one two three", encoding="utf-8")
print(word_count("assets/a.txt"))           # 3
print(word_count(Path("assets", "a.txt")))  # 3
print(word_count(Asset("a.txt")))           # 3

print(str(None))                            # None  -- a bogus "path"
try:
    os.fspath(None)
except TypeError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)                 # TypeError
takeaways: Accept `str | os.PathLike[str]` and convert with `Path(...)` once, at the top
Use `os.fspath` instead of `str()` when you need a string path
Return Path objects; don't let one parameter mean both a path and file contents
pitfalls: Using `str(path)` for conversion, which turns a stray None into a file literally named 'None'.

quiz.q: Why prefer os.fspath(p) over str(p) inside a function that takes a path?
options: It rejects objects that are not paths instead of silently stringifying them
quiz.explain: fspath only accepts str, bytes and os.PathLike, so mistakes surface as TypeError.

concepts.name: Subclassing Path and with_segments
concepts.summary: Extend Path with domain-specific methods using the 3.12+ subclassing support and with_segments.
concepts.why: Custom path types (project roots, paths in a virtual file system, paths carrying extra information) become clean, and type checkers can tell them apart.
concepts.body:
Before 3.12, subclassing `Path` was awkward because it handed work to `PosixPath`/`WindowsPath` internally. Since 3.12, `Path` and `PurePath` can be subclassed directly, and the subclass is kept in derived paths: `p / "x"`, `p.parent`, `p.iterdir()` and `p.glob()` all return instances of your class.

They do this through **with_segments(*pathsegments)**, which pathlib calls whenever it builds a new path from an existing one. The default creates `type(self)(*pathsegments)`. If your subclass carries extra state, such as a project base folder or a connection object (pick attribute names that don't clash with existing ones like `root`, `name` or `parts`), accept it in `__init__` and override `with_segments` to pass it along:

```python
def with_segments(self, *segments):
    return type(self)(*segments, base=self.base)
```

Since 3.12, `__init__` receives the path segments and you must call `super().__init__(*args)`; there's no need to override `__new__`.

Good uses: methods like `project_path.is_test_file()`, or a path type for a virtual file system. Keep subclasses thin; behaviour that doesn't depend on the path itself belongs elsewhere.

pathlib's internals changed a lot from 3.12 to 3.14 (`pathlib._abc`, `pathlib.types` in 3.14), so stick to documented hooks rather than private attributes.
takeaways: Since 3.12, Path subclasses survive /, parent, iterdir and glob
Override `with_segments` to carry extra state into derived paths
Call `super().__init__(*args)` and avoid private pathlib internals
pitfalls: Adding state in `__init__` but not overriding `with_segments`, so derived paths lose it and raise TypeError or AttributeError.

quiz.q: In Python 3.12+, what does (MyPath('a') / 'b') return when MyPath subclasses Path?
options: A MyPath instance, created via with_segments
quiz.explain: pathlib builds derived paths through with_segments, which by default uses type(self).

concepts.name: pathlib vs os: performance trade-offs
concepts.summary: Know where pathlib costs more than os and os.path, and how to keep loops over huge numbers of files fast.
concepts.why: Scanning millions of files with naive pathlib code can be several times slower than necessary.
concepts.body:
Path objects are convenient, but each one is a Python object that splits up and stores its parts, and many operations create new objects. In typical scripts this cost is tiny compared to reading from disk. It starts to matter when you touch hundreds of thousands of paths in a loop.

Where the time goes:

- **Repeated stat calls.** `p.is_file()`, `p.is_dir()` and `p.stat()` each ask the operating system for the file's details (a **stat** call). Calling all three per file triples the work. `os.scandir` returns `DirEntry` objects whose type is usually already known from the folder listing itself, with no extra call; `os.walk` and `Path.walk` build on it.
- **Object creation.** `root / name` for every entry creates a new Path and splits it up; joining strings is cheaper.
- **rglob over huge trees** that you'd prune anyway. Prefer `Path.walk` and prune.

Recent releases (3.12 and 3.13) rewrote `glob` internally for speed, so upgrading Python can itself help code that globs a lot.

Practical approach: write clear pathlib code first, then measure with a profiler. Only in the loop that runs for every file, switch to `os.scandir` and strings, converting results to Path at the end. Keeping one `stat()` result and reading several fields from it, instead of calling `stat()` again, also helps.
takeaways: Asking the operating system dominates: avoid repeated stat/is_file calls per entry
`os.scandir` reuses type info from the listing; os.walk and Path.walk build on it
Write pathlib first, measure, and drop to os.scandir only in the busiest loops
pitfalls: Calling `exists()`, `is_file()` and `stat()` on the same path in sequence inside a large loop.

quiz.q: Why is os.scandir with entry.is_file() typically faster than Path.iterdir with p.is_file()?
options: DirEntry usually knows the type from the listing, avoiding a stat call per file
Path objects are saved on disk
quiz.explain: The operating system reports entry types in the folder listing, and DirEntry keeps that information.
